summary: Specifies the Daytime service, which sends the current date and time as a character string without regard to the input. It is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it.

plainLanguage.summary: Ask a computer the time and it sends back a sentence with today's date and the hour.

subtitle: A service on port 13 that returns the current date and time as readable text.

tldr.problem: Engineers want a simple way to ask a host for its current date and time as human-readable text.
tldr.mechanism: A server on port 13 sends the date and time as an ASCII string, over TCP followed by closing the connection, or in one UDP datagram. Received data is ignored.
tldr.outcome: The RFC is an Internet Standard for hosts that choose to implement it. It points to the Time Protocol, RFC 868, for a machine-usable time.

today: RFC 867 is an Internet Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of the Daytime Protocol.

sections.title: A Daytime Service
sections.content:
RFC 867 defines the Daytime Protocol. The RFC calls a daytime service a useful debugging and measurement tool that simply sends the current date and time as a character string without regard to the input.

Hosts on the ARPA Internet that choose to implement it are expected to adopt this standard.
sections.plainLanguage: It is a machine that tells you the date and time in plain words, whatever you ask it.

sections.title: The TCP and UDP Services
sections.content:
Over TCP, a server listens on TCP port 13. Once a connection is established it sends the current date and time as an ASCII character string and discards any data received. The service then closes the connection.

Over UDP, a server listens on UDP port 13. When a datagram is received, it sends an answering datagram containing the date and time as an ASCII string, ignoring the received data.
sections.plainLanguage: You connect or send a note, and the machine writes back the time as a sentence.

sections.title: Daytime Syntax
sections.content:
There is no specific syntax for the daytime. The RFC recommends limiting it to the ASCII printing characters, space, carriage return and line feed, and keeping it to one line.

One popular syntax is Weekday, Month Day, Year Time-Zone, for example Tuesday, February 22, 1982 17:37:43-PST. Another is the one used in SMTP, dd mmm yy hh:mm:ss zzz, for example 02 FEB 82 07:59:01 PST.

The RFC adds a note: for a machine-useful time, use the Time Protocol (RFC 868).
sections.plainLanguage: The time is written the way a person would say it. If another computer needs the time as a number, it should use the Time Protocol instead.

references.text: Time Protocol, RFC 868, referenced in the note on machine-useful time.
